book: 166 - Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book

chapters.relation: The editors' introduction explains why Green Lantern merits a philosophy volume: an intergalactic corps of different species that must cooperate, rings limited only by willpower and imagination, and a cast (Hal, Kyle, John, Guy, Sinestro, Mogo, Soranik Natu) dense with philosophical questions. It frames the book's guiding problems: what limits justice places on the ring, whether a Green Lantern can do literally anything, and how the color-coded emotional spectrum should affect judgment and decision-making.

Southworth uses the War of Light to ask what role emotion should play in moral reasoning: Sinestro rules Korugar through fear, the Star Sapphires kidnap Sinestro Corps prisoners to convert them to love, Atrocitus's rage was forged by the Manhunters' massacre, Larfleeze hoards, and the Blue Lanterns merely hope that hope matters. On Aristotle's account every corps errs by excess: Atrocitus's rage makes him miss chances to kill Sinestro, Fatality's love benches John Stewart from saving his friends, and even the Green Lanterns' will-only ideal fails, since total fearlessness is itself vicious and Plato's picture has reason directing emotion like a general directing soldiers. He ends by defending Mill's utilitarianism: the Guardians' real failure was not detachment but pretending to be detached, and reading them as flawed 'benevolent, disinterested spectators' vindicates the Corps while explaining their moral growth after Scar and the Blackest Night.

White asks whether Sinestro's quip that Hal's mind is 'like a muscle unused for years' is a mere metaphor and argues willpower is a real, exercisable strength. Against the Humean desire-belief model, which cannot explain Tom Kalamaku fixing planes instead of browsing Facebook, he uses Searle's 'gaps' to locate an independent will that can choose against one's better judgment, and Kant's account of virtue as moral strength in fulfilling duty despite inclination. Holton and Baumeister's findings that self-control depletes and strengthens like a muscle fit the comics exactly: Ollie is exhausted by a single ring use in Rebirth, Hal sweats through moving a planet, and John Stewart must 'suppress my own terrors' to hold the Mosaic walls.

Donovan and Richardson read the Maltusian split, with the male Guardians banning emotion through the Book of Oa on Oa and the female Zamarons leaving to found the violet light of love on Zamaron, as the Western association of men with reason and women with emotion. They deploy Gilligan's different-voice reply to Kohlberg, the Pythagorean table of opposites via Genevieve Lloyd, Hegel's exclusion of women from the public sphere, and Jaggar's liberal-feminist critique of 'ahistorical' reason, whose comic-book analogue is the third law banning relationships between Lanterns. The chapter ends by arguing the standoff is a false dichotomy the comics themselves begin to dissolve: Kyle's 'Lanterns with heart' speech to the Guardians, the repeal of the third law, and the Indigo Tribe's plan to recombine the seven corps into the white light of creation.

Terjesen asks how Sinestro and Universo ever passed recruitment and answers that the Guardians' two-prong test of honesty and fearlessness reflects moral pluralism: universal rules kept deliberately thin so that different moral codes can coexist, which is why the vicious 'good bad man' Jack T. Chance keeps his ring on Hellhole. But honor, honesty, and justice are thick ethical concepts in Bernard Williams's sense, requiring cultural context to apply, so Laira's execution of a surrendered Amon Sur and the Guardians' own cover-ups (the Corpse, Kentor Omoto) cannot be settled by appealing to thin 'justice,' and the Alpha Lanterns' internal-affairs role cannot fix it. Moral particularism leaves the Corps with unresolvable disagreements about who the bad apples are.

Dryden reads Hal and Sinestro through Hegel's account of the tragic hero: each acts from a one-sided individual moral compass (Hal rebuilding Coast City in Emerald Twilight and trying to reboot the universe in Zero Hour; Sinestro dictating order to Korugar), collides with communal ethical life, and is destroyed, yet stays aesthetically admirable for the magnificence of the commitment. Fichte's planned police state of ID cards, registered addresses, and total surveillance is exactly the order Sinestro would have liked, the scheme Hegel mocked as tyranny. Kyle escapes the tragic pattern because fear and self-doubt keep him responsive to his groups' shared values, making him 'corps conscience' rather than 'the greatest.'

Michaud argues Hal is a murderer who should not be forgiven for Emerald Twilight even though the Parallax retcon blames a fear entity. Using Frankfurt's cases (a parasite that would force you to rob a bank you were already choosing to rob), he shows that lacking alternatives does not excuse, then applies Fischer and Ravizza: Hal's rampage issued from his own reasons-responsive mechanism ('it was still my hand that did it'), so he had guidance control. Since Hal's willpower later let him resist Parallax to reignite the sun in Final Night, Michaud concludes he likely had regulative control too, and that absolving him insults the very will that made him the greatest Lantern.

Darowski traces Hal's shifting motivations across fifty years: the Showcase #22 origin where honesty and fearlessness make heroism a simple vow, the selfish Parallax era after Coast City's destruction, the Spectre's atonement, and the guilt-driven Lantern of Rebirth. Plato's claim that knowing the good suffices for doing good would mean Hal never really chose heroism, but the chapter rejects it, since morality alone failed to stop Hal's turn to Parallax. Set against the darker post-Watchmen industry, it asks whether guilt-driven atonement is a nobler motive than simple duty and what standards we should hold heroes to.

Terjesen reads the O'Neil-Adams pairing as moral rationalism (Hal) versus moral sentimentalism (Ollie): Hal jails the boy assaulting slumlord Jubal Slade because 'He was breaking the law' and defends a racist senator's speech on free-speech principle, while Ollie works from the gut. Hume's 'Reason is and ought only to be the slave of the passions' explains both Ollie's effectiveness and Hal's collapse into Parallax, since no argument from Kilowog could restrain a grief only a stronger passion could. But sentiment needs an impartial filter: Smith's impartial spectator condemns Ollie's near-murder of Black Canary's attacker and his abandonment of the heroin-addicted Speedy, while Hal's cooler principle keeps the Native American land dispute from Ollie's violent plan. The conclusion is that morality is sentiment-based but reason must police it, so each hero needs the other.

Patterson maps the Comics Code censorship debate onto Plato's Republic Book X, where imitative art is thrice removed from the Forms (the god's table, the carpenter's table, the painter's picture) and feeds the passionate soul, versus Aristotle's Poetics, where imitation is natural and tragedy's pity and fear yield catharsis. The O'Neil-Adams run embodies Aristotle: the slum story where a black tenant asks why Green Lantern helps 'orange skins' and 'purple skins' but never 'black skins,' the Ulysses Star land dispute, and Speedy's heroin addiction broke Code taboos so readers would learn from engagement rather than distance. Within the comic, Hal plays the establishment Platonist who would change an unjust law rather than disobey it and Green Arrow the Aristotelian activist, so their friendship dramatizes the ancient quarrel over whether art corrupts or teaches.

Dryden asks whether the Lanterns' relationships are weaknesses or strengths. Epictetus's dichotomy of control would have recruits greet the Sinestro Corps' display of their families' eyeballs with Stoic indifference, and Kant brands fear for loved ones heteronomous; yet Donna Parker refuses the ring for her children, Amnee and Matoo Pree surrender their rings rather than stop loving, and Kilowog dines with energy constructs of his dead family, showing attachments partly constitute who people are. Feminist relational autonomy resolves the tension: Kyle escapes Parallax only by grasping Hal's hand ('we don't have to do it alone'), and Soranik Natu cannot excise Sinestro's crest or parentage any more than Donchin's Huntington's-disease daughter can sever family ties, so autonomy competency means negotiating unchosen relationships rather than escaping them.

Tallman and Southworth set the Hippocratic Oath against the Green Lantern oath in Soranik Natu, a Korugarian surgeon who must either stop healing mid-battle or disobey the Book of Oa. They survey the options, with Wonder Woman discarding vows for consequences, Isamot Kol letting the Corps trump his vow to Qalyra, Dr. Mid-Nite always putting patients first, and Dick Grayson going by context, then argue through Hursthouse that Natu, who treats both oaths as absolute, is in an irresolvable dilemma of her own making, more like the double-betrothed man than Williams's tragic Jim and the twenty Indians. Their verdict is that she should turn in the ring, a cautionary tale for real military medics whose oaths also collide.

White distinguishes retributivism from deterrence and rehabilitation through the Corps' execution vote on Sinestro and Fatality's lex talionis pursuit of John Stewart over Xanshi ('You have four billion eyes to account for'). Kant grounds retribution in dignity, so punishment must treat the criminal as an end, never merely as a means to deterrence, and is owed to him for his crime ('You did this to yourself,' Hal tells Sinestro), while Hegel adds that punishment annuls the crime and embodies the criminal's own right. Feinberg's expressive theory explains the Korugarian crowd that felt 'cheated of Korugar's redemption' when the execution stalled, and the chapter closes by separating justice from vengeance: Ollie's arrow through Prometheus and Laira's 'It was justice!' killing of a surrendered Amon Sur were personal revenge, which only impartial state agents may convert into justice.

Novy uses Terry Berg's gay-bashing coma in 'Brother's Keeper' to argue hate crimes are a kind of terrorism: justice, in Iris Marion Young's enabling sense, requires social conditions in which citizens can develop and exercise their capacities, and an attack that makes every gay teenager police holding hands in public harms the whole group, so Mill's greatest-happiness principle and Feinberg's expressivism justify enhanced penalties. The chapter then turns on Kyle, who tortures Daniel Hirsh on Rikers Island and nearly beats his two accomplices to death, asking whether extraordinary crimes justify extraordinary procedures in a post-9/11 world. Kyle's horror afterward, begging Flash to undo the last twenty-four hours and losing his will to protect, and Batman's pointed 'But that is me, isn't it?' mark the line between punishing brutality and becoming it.

Barkman retells Glaucon's Ring of Gyges, a shepherd's invisibility ring used to seduce the queen and murder the king, as Lord Acton's claim that absolute power corrupts, and answers with Plato: injustice disorders the tripartite soul, so the unjust sacrifice the happiness that matters most. The Guardians of the Universe are Plato's guardians writ cosmic, wise enough to rule themselves; Yalan Gur fell only when the yellow weakness was removed from his ring, Sinestro never had the wisdom ('You have never understood us'), and Hal's lapses, resigning for Carol Ferris and the Emerald Twilight rampage, are ignorance of the proper value of things rather than evil, since 'Hal's not evil... He believes he's acting for the right reasons.' The power ring is a modern Ring of Gyges, and Plato's test explains both who passes it and who fails.

Finkelman uses the Corps' strangest members, Mogo the sentient planet, Leezle Pon the smallpox virus, the billion-puffball Collective, and Dkrtzy RRR the mathematical equation, to run the philosophy-of-biology debate over what counts as an individual. Plato's 'carving nature at its joints' frames the question; Heraclitean flux and Parmenidean changelessness picture monism's extremes; Aristotle's substance and soul deny Mogo is a living individual since its ecosystems (the Resal) do not serve it as organs serve a body; Darwin's natural selection makes organisms the real units, with Sinestro's attacks a kind of artificial selection that adapted the Corps. Gene reductionism (George C. Williams and Dawkins) versus Gould's contextual pluralism then decides how to count one billion puffballs as one Lantern.

Jaissle reads the Book of Oa as Peirce's communal mind made physical: Kyle's ring translates the sounds of sector 3599 only because language 1,456 is already cataloged by the community, and even the Guardians cannot translate Hal's cursing until some Lantern has heard it. Because the individual apart from his fellows 'is only a negation,' the Guardians' deletion of the Blackest Night prophecy from the Book shows the fallibility of even immortal individual minds, while the Corps' shared experience across the War of Light vindicated the Cosmic Revelations. The green light beats the emotion-driven corps because willpower uniquely balances individual agency with communal knowledge.

Kind uses John Stewart's Justice League arc, thrown into the future by Chronos, meeting his son Warhawk, and hiding it from Hawkgirl while dating Vixen, to stage fatalism: Pike and Taylor's arguments that a foreknown future, whether God's or a time traveler's, cannot be otherwise. Time travel itself forces a choice between presentism and eternalism, since Warhawk must 'exist now, already, in the future' for GL and Batman to visit him, and Smart's tenseless four-dimensionalism, with GL a series of timeslices and 'now' as subjective as 'here,' dissolves the fatalist worry by banishing tensed facts. The chapter lands on GL's battlefield advice to his son: 'Plant your feet,' owning a fate you cannot escape.

Malloy explains Hal's endless giant hands and boxing gloves as an inherent limit of imagination rather than lazy writing: only the self-contradictory (square circles, married bachelors) cannot be imagined at all, and on Hume's empiricism imagination merely recombines copies of impressions, ideas, by the associations of contiguity, resemblance, and cause and effect, so Hal reproduces his most deeply impressed, most ordinary experiences. James's 'living options' bound what is worth imagining, and Kyle's JLA speed-to-sound machine shows invention's two stages: the experience-limited Lantern supplies the idea while the semisentient ring handles execution. The upshot is advice to go out and make new impressions.

Nielsen asks whether a Green Lantern with unlimited willpower would be a god and answers no through Leibniz: God is the absolutely perfect being, where perfection excludes contradiction so that knowledge and power admit of perfection but 'the greatest of all numbers' does not, and such a being creates the best of all possible worlds. Hume's trilemma (impotent, malevolent, or whence evil?) is met with the theodicy that finite minds, like Lanterns baffled by Guardian decrees, cannot compare our world to the discarded possibilities, each perhaps as bad as Qward. Since omnipotence requires omniscience and omnibenevolence, not even Parallax, the Anti-Monitor, or Kyle as Ion counts as omnipotent: admirable and powerful, but not gods.

Jones tests Clarke's law, that any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic, against the mythos's two green power sources: the Guardians' scientific Central Power Battery and the Starheart, the wild magic they quarantined, which later made Alan Scott's body pure green flame. Mauss's distinctions (magic private and rule-bound, religion communal and belief-powered, science open and collaborative) show the Guardians operate like sorcerers rather than scientists, secretive and incurious, while Kyle's Rebirth speech on the emotional electromagnetic spectrum explains why only willpower, the balancing center of the spectrum, can keep order where rage, fear, or love cannot.

holes.name: Thick and Thin Ethical Concepts
holes.what: Williams's distinction between context-dependent value concepts like honor and honesty (thick) and context-free ones like right and just (thin).
holes.why: Chapter 13's account of why the Guardians cannot vet recruits or judge Laira rests entirely on honor and justice being thick concepts.

holes.name: Moral Particularism
holes.what: The view, associated with Jonathan Dancy, that moral judgment proceeds from case-by-case perception of particulars rather than invariant principles.
holes.why: Chapter 13 argues the Alpha Lanterns cannot supply context-free justice because no moral judgment avoids thick concepts.

holes.name: Moral Pluralism
holes.what: The view that there are several valid conceptions of the good, positioned between relativism and absolutism.
holes.why: Chapter 13 defines the Guardians' recruitment policy as moral pluralism, explicitly distinguished in the text from the relativism the taxonomy names.

holes.name: Hegel on Tragedy and Ethical Life (Sittlichkeit)
holes.what: Hegel's account of the tragic hero destroyed by one-sided individual moral conviction set against communal ethical life, yet aesthetically admirable.
holes.why: Chapter 14 reads Hal, Sinestro, and Kyle entirely through this pattern; none of the existing Hegel slugs (dialectic, master-slave, Geist, history, recognition) covers it.

holes.name: Guidance Control (Fischer and Ravizza)
holes.what: Fischer and Ravizza's compatibilist criterion of moral responsibility: ownership of one's action plus reasons-responsiveness, rather than the ability to do otherwise.
holes.why: Chapter 15's verdict that Hal is blameworthy under Parallax turns on guidance control versus regulative control; the generic compatibilism slug is too coarse.

holes.name: Catharsis (Poetics)
holes.what: Aristotle's account of tragedy arousing pity and fear in order to purge or refine those emotions in the audience.
holes.why: Chapter 19 needs it as Aristotle's half of the censorship debate against Plato's banishment of the poets, applied to the Comics Code and the O'Neil-Adams run.

holes.name: Relational Autonomy
holes.what: The feminist reworking of autonomy (Nedelsky, Mackenzie and Stoljar) on which relationships partly constitute the self rather than merely threatening self-determination.
holes.why: Chapter 20 argues Kyle escapes Parallax only with Hal's help and that Corps life demands autonomy competency within unchosen relationships.

holes.name: Irresolvable and Tragic Moral Dilemmas
holes.what: Situations (Hursthouse, building on Williams's Jim case) in which every available action violates a duty and leaves moral residue no matter what the agent does.
holes.why: Chapter 22 argues Soranik Natu's Hippocratic and Lantern oaths create exactly such an irresolvable dilemma; no existing slug names it.

holes.name: Biological Individuality and the Superorganism
holes.what: The philosophy-of-biology question of which levels of the living hierarchy (genes, organisms, species, superorganisms) count as real individuals.
holes.why: Chapter 27 runs this whole debate through Mogo, the Collective, and Leezle Pon, and the taxonomy has no philosophy-of-biology concept.

holes.name: Peirce's Communal Mind
holes.what: Peirce's view that thought is a semiotic process not tied to any brain and that knowledge and truth are established only by an unlimited community of inquirers.
holes.why: Chapter 28 maps the Book of Oa and the Corps' shared ring knowledge onto it directly, and the existing Peirce slug (pragmatic method) does not cover it.

holes.name: Impressions, Ideas and the Principles of Association
holes.what: Hume's empiricist theory that thinking copies sensory impressions into ideas and recombines them by contiguity, resemblance, and cause and effect.
holes.why: Chapter 31 explains Hal's boxing-glove constructs and Kyle's inventions entirely through this machinery, which no existing Hume slug covers.

holes.name: Magic, Science and Religion (Mauss)
holes.what: Mauss's sociological demarcation of magic as private, rule-bound, and will-powered, against communal religion and open, collaborative science.
holes.why: Chapter 33 uses this triad, plus Clarke's three laws, to decide whether the Guardians are scientists or sorcerers; the taxonomy has nothing on the demarcation.
